description: Life in 1337: the parish, the manor, the wool trade and the gulf between rich and poor.
content_html:
England on the Eve of War

In 1337, England was a deeply ordered society. Most people never travelled more than a few miles from their birthplace, and their lives were shaped by three interlocking institutions: the manor, the parish church, and the serf system that kept most people tied to the land. Understanding this world is essential because the crises of plague and revolt that followed make little sense without it.

The Manorial System

English rural life was organised around the manorial system. At its head stood the lord of the manor, who owned the land and administered justice through the manorial court. Beneath him were free tenants who paid rent in money, and below them the villeins — unfree peasants who owed their lord a set number of days’ work each week on the lord’s “demesne” land. In return they were given strips of land to farm for themselves.

Serfdom was the defining reality of most people’s lives. A serf could not leave the manor, marry without the lord’s permission, or pass on their land freely. They were legally his property. Historians estimate that roughly half of England’s rural population in the early fourteenth century were villeins or serfs bound to manors in this way.

Key Fact

A villein (serf) could not leave the manor, marry, or pass on land without the lord’s permission. They owed labour — typically two to three days per week on the lord’s demesne — as well as rents in grain or money.

The Role of the Church

No institution touched everyday life as deeply as the parish church. The parish was the centre of the community — it recorded births, marriages and deaths, provided charity, and gave the agricultural year its rhythm through the great festivals: Christmas, Easter, Midsummer and Harvest. In a largely illiterate society, the priest was one of the few educated men most people would ever meet.

The Church was also enormously wealthy. By the fourteenth century the Church owned roughly a third of all land in England. Monasteries, cathedrals and parish churches collected tithes — a tenth of each parishioner’s produce — as well as fees for baptisms, marriages and burials. This wealth made the Church a powerful landlord as well as a spiritual authority.

Faith shaped how people understood suffering, illness and death. Disease was widely seen as God’s punishment for sin, and the only remedies available were prayer, pilgrimage and the sacraments of the Church. This worldview would become dangerously important when the Black Death arrived in 1348.

The Church commanded unquestioned authority at every level of society. The Pope in Rome claimed spiritual supremacy over all Christian kingdoms, and English bishops sat in the House of Lords alongside the great nobles. The Archbishop of Canterbury was among the most powerful men in the kingdom.

Yet the Church faced growing criticism. Some priests were poorly educated or corrupt, collecting tithes without providing adequate spiritual care. Wealthy monasteries attracted accusations of greed. These tensions would deepen over the fourteenth century — John Wyclif’s later challenges to Church authority did not come from nowhere but built on long-standing popular resentment.

The Wool Trade

England’s greatest source of wealth in the fourteenth century was wool. English wool trade supplied the looms of Flanders (modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands), where it was woven into fine cloth and sold across Europe. By the 1330s, England exported around 30,000 sacks of wool per year, generating enormous customs revenue for the Crown.

The wool trade shaped politics as well as economics. Edward III desperately needed the revenue from wool customs to fund his wars in France. He also needed the goodwill of Flemish merchants and cloth-workers — which partly explains why the Flemish towns’ preference for English wool made them potential allies against France. The relationship between trade and war was close and constant throughout this period.

Key Fact

Wool was England’s most valuable export. Customs duties on wool provided a significant share of royal income, and the Flemish cloth industry’s dependence on English wool gave Edward III diplomatic leverage when seeking allies against France.

The Position of Women

Women in fourteenth-century England occupied a legally inferior position. Under common law, married women had no separate legal identity — they could not own property, make contracts, or bring lawsuits in their own name. A wife’s legal person was absorbed into her husband’s.

In practice, life was more complex. Peasant women worked alongside men in the fields, as well as spinning, brewing, baking and managing the household. Widows could hold land and run businesses in their own right. Women in towns sometimes worked in trades and crafts, sometimes as independent traders known as “femmes soles.” Noble women could manage vast estates in their husbands’ absence. Yet access to education, the Church hierarchy and political power remained entirely closed to women at every level of society.

The gap between rich and poor in fourteenth-century England was enormous. A great baron might command thousands of acres and dozens of dependent manors; a villein family scratched a living from a few strips of land subject to weather, disease and the lord’s arbitrary demands. The nobility and gentry ate varied diets rich in meat and imported spices; peasants depended on bread, pottage and ale, with meat a rare luxury.

Yet the system was not entirely static. Some free peasants accumulated land and became prosperous yeomen. Skilled tradesmen in towns could rise to modest comfort. The wool trade created a new merchant class whose wealth rivalled that of minor nobles — and who would become increasingly influential in Parliament. It was this social complexity — people with grievances, aspirations and some leverage — that would make the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 possible.
exam_tip_html: For “describe two features” questions about medieval English society, you need to make two separate, specific points — not two aspects of the same point. For example, “the Church was wealthy” and “the Church provided education through priests” are two features; “the Church was powerful and influential” is one feature expressed twice. On 6-mark “explain a cause” questions about the Peasants’ Revolt, always anchor your explanation in specific features of medieval society covered here — serfdom, the Church’s power, the gap between rich and poor — to show you understand the context, not just the trigger events.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval England in 1337 was shaped by the manorial system: lords owned the land, villeins owed labour, and serfdom kept roughly half the rural population legally bound to their lord’s estate.
  • The parish church was the centre of community life and enormous institutional wealth, owning around a third of all English land and collecting tithes from every parishioner.
  • The wool trade was England’s economic engine, funding royal wars and creating diplomatic leverage, while the huge gap between rich and poor built up the tensions that would later explode in revolt.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the manorial system in fourteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. One mark for a simple identification, two marks for a developed feature. Example: Villeins owed their lord a set number of days of labour each week on the demesne land [1], and in return received strips of land to farm for their own subsistence [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Church's role in medieval English society.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for a simple point, 2 for a developed point). Feature 1: The Church was the centre of community life, marking births, marriages and deaths through the parish system [1] and providing charity and the rhythm of the agricultural year through religious festivals [1]. Feature 2: The Church was enormously wealthy, owning roughly a third of all English land by the fourteenth century [1] and collecting tithes — a tenth of each parishioner's produce — as compulsory income [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the tension between rich and poor in fourteenth-century England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific cause (e.g. serfdom, the Church's landholding, labour obligations) and explains it in depth, linking it to broader inequalities in medieval society with precise factual support. Secure: Identifies a cause and explains it with some factual detail. Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to inequality without a specific cause identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of England's dependence on the wool trade in the 1330s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a specific consequence (e.g. Crown reliance on wool customs for war finance, diplomatic ties to Flemish towns, growth of a merchant class) and explains it in depth with factual support, showing how it shaped Edward III's decisions. Secure: Identifies a consequence and explains it with relevant factual support. Developing: States a consequence with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague point without specific factual detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of serfdom to an understanding of the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance both at the time (serfdom created resentment, bound people to land, restricted freedom and wages) and over time (the revolt accelerated serfdom's decline; the issue of bound labour remained contested into the fifteenth century). Precise factual knowledge integrated throughout. Secure: Explains significance at the time with some reference to longer-term impact. Developing: Describes features of serfdom without clearly linking to its significance. Emerging: Limited factual knowledge; significance not addressed.

practice_questions.text:
'The position of the Church was the most important feature of English society in 1337.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
Use your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with the interpretation using precise factual knowledge. Agrees: Church owned ~one third of land, collected tithes, shaped daily life through parishes and festivals, held political power via bishops in the Lords. Disagrees: The manorial system and serfdom were arguably more important to most people's lives; the wool trade drove royal policy and shaped alliances. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may lack full development. Developing: Describes features without clearly evaluating the interpretation. Emerging: Simple descriptive response; no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes an unfree peasant legally bound to a lord's manor in medieval England?
Roughly what fraction of all English land did the Church own by the fourteenth century?
England's most valuable export in the fourteenth century was _____, which funded royal wars and supplied Flemish weavers.
The _____ was the basic unit of community and religious life in medieval England, where births, marriages and deaths were all recorded.
Match each group to their position in medieval English society:
right: Bought English wool for weaving into cloth
Unfree peasants owing labour to a lord
Owned roughly a third of England's land

flashcard_questions.q: What was a villein in medieval England?
flashcard_questions.a: An unfree peasant legally bound to a lord's manor, unable to leave without permission.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the 'demesne' in the manorial system?
flashcard_questions.a: The lord's own land, farmed by villeins as part of their labour obligations.

flashcard_questions.q: Roughly how many days per week did a typical villein owe their lord in labour?
flashcard_questions.a: Two to three days per week.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Hundred Years' War begin, placing England in 1337?
What fraction of English land did the Church own by the fourteenth century?

flashcard_questions.a: A compulsory payment of one tenth of a parishioner's annual produce to the Church.

flashcard_questions.q: What was England's most valuable export in the fourteenth century?
flashcard_questions.a: Wool, sold to Flemish weavers in Flanders.

flashcard_questions.q: Why did the wool trade matter to Edward III's war plans?
flashcard_questions.a: Wool customs provided royal income and Flemish towns' dependence gave him diplomatic leverage against France.

flashcard_questions.q: What legal restriction applied to married women in fourteenth-century England?
flashcard_questions.a: They had no separate legal identity — they could not own property or make contracts in their own name.

flashcard_questions.q: What was a 'femme sole' in medieval England?
flashcard_questions.a: A woman trading independently, usually a widow or unmarried woman with her own legal standing in trade.

flashcard_questions.q: What did illness and disease typically mean to fourteenth-century English people?
flashcard_questions.a: God's punishment for sin, to be met with prayer, pilgrimage and the sacraments.

flashcard_questions.q: The ____ system bound peasants to the land and required labour on the lord's estate.

glossary_terms.definition: The estate of a lord, farmed by peasants who owed labour and rent in return for land and protection.
A class of unfree peasants legally bound to the land of their lord, unable to leave without permission.
The social and economic system in which lords granted land to peasants who owed labour services and loyalty in return.
The local church that served a defined community, the basic unit of Christian life in medieval England.
Raw or spun wool exported from England to Flemish weavers, the foundation of England's medieval trading wealth.
